passage:
Yamini's sketchbook was hidden under the mattress again. Papa had found it last month and said, very quietly, "Science, Yamini. Or don't call yourself our daughter. What will the family say if you draw cartoons for a living?"
He wasn't shouting. He never shouted. He paid for her tuition, sat up with her before exams, brought her favourite jalebis every Friday. That was what made it so confusing.
On the building terrace, she showed a new drawing to Yusuf, who lived two floors down and was in his first year of design college.
"It's really good," he said. "Why do you look scared?"
"Because I love them," Yamini said. "And every time I pick up a pencil, it feels like I'm choosing to lose them."
Yusuf didn't tell her what to do. He only said, "Maybe the school counsellor could help you talk to them. You shouldn't have to carry this alone."

qa.q: Where was Yamini's sketchbook hidden?
qa.a: It was hidden under the mattress again.

qa.q: Why does picking up a pencil feel like losing them to Yamini?
qa.a: She loves them deeply, and Papa's warning made drawing feel like choosing to be cut off, so love and freedom pull against each other.

qa.q: What small step could help Yamini now?
qa.a: She could take up Yusuf's idea and ask the school counsellor to help her talk to Papa and the family, so she isn't carrying the pressure alone.

qa.q: How might Papa see his warning about science?
qa.a: He probably sees it as care and duty, protecting her future and the family's name, without noticing how frightening the threat feels to her.

grounding: A girl whose loving father threatens shame and disowning over her wish to draw feels torn between love and freedom.

"Where were you till six?" Madhuri asked, not looking up from the rotis.
"At Neha's. Project work, Amma."
"I told you. That girl is a distraction. People talk."
"Neha's my best friend. What people?"
"Your aunties. Your grandmother. You want them saying I raised a girl who roams around?" Amma finally looked up. "If you go there again, don't expect me to fight for your hostel next year."
Vidya's throat tightened. "That's not fair."
"Fair?" Amma's voice softened. "I lie awake worrying every night. I do everything for you. This is for your own good, kanna."
Vidya stood there, torn. Amma's hands were floury, her eyes tired and full of love. Vidya wanted to hug her. She also wanted to scream.
"Okay," she said. She went to her room and texted Neha: can't come tmrw. sorry. will explain.
Then she sat on the bed, not sure what she would explain.

qa.q: Whose house was Vidya at until six?
qa.a: Vidya was at Neha's house, doing project work.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she stood there?
qa.a: She felt torn, wanting to hug Amma for her tired, loving eyes and also wanting to scream at the unfair threat.

qa.q: What could Vidya do after texting Neha?
qa.a: She could talk to a trusted adult outside the argument, like a school counsellor, about how to speak calmly with Amma about her friendship.

qa.q: How does Madhuri see her own rule?
qa.a: Madhuri sees it as worry and love, for Vidya's own good, shaped by fear of what relatives will say, not as control.

grounding: A girl whose loving mother threatens to withdraw support if she keeps seeing her best friend feels torn between love and freedom.

"Papa, I want to take arts after Class 10. History and political science."
Jagdish put down his newspaper. "Arts? Lalit, what will I tell your uncles? Everyone's son is doing science."
"I'm not everyone's son."
"If you do this, don't expect me to face the family at the wedding. You'll bring shame on all of us."
Lalit's throat tightened. "It's my life, Papa."
"Your life? Who paid for your tuition? Who sat with you all night when you had fever?" His voice cracked. "I only want what's best for you."
Lalit looked at his father's tired eyes. He did sit up all those nights. He did love him. And he was also saying: choose, or lose us.
"Can I think about it?" Lalit said quietly.
"Think. But remember what I said."
Lalit went to his room and stared at the ceiling, confused about where love ended and control began.

qa.q: What subjects does Lalit want to take?
qa.a: History and political science.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel as he stares at the ceiling?
qa.a: Lalit feels torn and confused, loving his father and grateful for his care, but pressured by the threat of shame and losing the family's approval.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next to get support?
qa.a: Lalit could talk to the school counsellor or a respected relative who could help him and his father discuss his choice calmly.

qa.q: How does Jagdish seem to see his own words?
qa.a: Jagdish seems to see them as love and duty, wanting the best for his son, without seeing how much they pressure Lalit.

grounding: It shows a teenager torn between love for his father and freedom to choose his subjects, when care comes with threats of shame.

passage:
My name is Bidisha, I'm fifteen, and I love my brother Chinmay more than almost anyone.
He taught me to ride a cycle. He brings me my favourite sweets from the station every Friday. When I was sick last year, he slept on the floor beside my bed.
He also checks my phone every night. He decides which friends I can visit. When I talked to a boy from my tuition about homework, he said, "Our family's name matters. If you shame us, I'll never speak to you again." Then he hugged me.
I don't know what to call it. It feels like love and a cage at the same time. When I try to explain it to friends, it sounds either too good or too bad.
Last week, I told our school counsellor. She listened, and then she said, "It's possible to love someone and still need your own freedom." I cried, because that was exactly it.

qa.q: What does Chinmay bring Bidisha every Friday?
qa.a: He brings Bidisha's favourite sweets from the station.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel about her brother?
qa.a: Bidisha feels deep affection for him and also trapped and confused, as if his love and control are a cage at the same time.

qa.q: What step did Bidisha take that helped?
qa.a: Bidisha told the school counsellor, who listened and named that love and the need for freedom can exist together.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see his checking and rules?
qa.a: Chinmay probably sees them as protecting the family name and Bidisha, not as control.

grounding: It shows a teenager loved and controlled by a brother through threats of shame and cutting ties, confused because care and control come together.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, written by Jaya, Monday.
Sabina came to me after the prayer assembly, very quiet. Her parents have arranged her engagement to a relative for after her board exams. She is fifteen. She said, "They say if I refuse, I'm not their daughter anymore."
She also said her mother cries at night worrying about her future, and her father works two jobs to pay her fees. "They love me," she kept saying. "I know they do."
I told her she is not to blame for any of this, and that her feelings of love and fear can both be true.
Because this concerns a child's safety and the law, I informed our safeguarding lead immediately, and we called the child helpline together this afternoon. The helpline will visit the family with a local official. Sabina knows I will check on her every morning this week.

qa.q: When is Sabina's engagement arranged for?
qa.a: For after her board exams.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel about her parents?
qa.a: Sabina feels loving and loyal toward them, but frightened of being cut off if she refuses the engagement.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do the same day?
qa.a: The counsellor told Sabina she was not to blame, informed the safeguarding lead immediately, and called the child helpline that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Sabina's parents see the engagement?
qa.a: Her parents may see it as securing her future out of love and worry, not as control or harm.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenager whose loving family controls her future with threats of cutting ties, and acts the same day to protect her.

Wednesday
Papa found out I'd filled in the form for the arts stream and not science. He didn't shout. He said, very quietly, "If you do this, don't tell anyone you're my daughter. The whole family will be laughed at." Then he went to his room. Ma sat with me and said, "He only wants your good. You know how much he loves you."
And he does. He wakes at five to drop me at tuition. He saved for years for my laptop. That's what makes it so confusing. The same person who loves me is the one making me feel ashamed of the thing I actually want.
Bhupen-dada came in later and sat on the floor. He said, "You're allowed to love him and still want your own life." I cried into my pillow after he left.
I haven't torn up the form. Tomorrow I'll ask Mrs Kharkongor if she can talk to us together.
Minakshi

qa.q: Which stream had Minakshi filled in the form for?
qa.a: The arts stream, not science.

qa.q: Why does Minakshi feel so confused?
qa.a: Minakshi feels torn and ashamed, because the same Papa who loves her and wakes at five for her is the one threatening shame over what she wants.

qa.q: What small step is Minakshi planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Mrs Kharkongor to talk to the family together brings in a respected outside adult who can help the conversation without it becoming a fight.

qa.q: How does Bhupen-dada see Minakshi's situation?
qa.a: Bhupen-dada seems to understand the pull of both love and freedom, telling Minakshi it is allowed to love Papa and still want her own life.

grounding: Shows a young person whose loving family controls her choice of study with the threat of shame, leaving her torn between love and freedom.
